chapters.hook_a: From a third to three quarters

lines.note: Poland: 30% of Germany's level in 1990, 75% in 2025
lines.say: In 1990, the average Pole produced less than a third of what the average German did. Today, it's three quarters.
On the way, Poland overtook Hungary, Greece and Portugal, and it's now within five percent of Spain.
This is how it happened, in thirty-five years of numbers, and what those numbers don't show.

card: GDP per person, adjusted for inflation and for prices in each country. Source: World Bank
lines.say: First, what we're measuring. This is GDP per person: the value of everything a country produces in a year, divided by its population. It's in constant international dollars, which take out both inflation and the differences in what things cost from one country to another.

card: It doesn't say who gets the money, or how many hours it takes to earn it
lines.say: It's the standard way to compare average living standards between countries. It isn't everything: it doesn't tell you who gets the money, or how many hours people work for it. We'll come back to that.

card: Germany, France, the UK, Italy · Spain, Portugal, Greece · Czechia, Hungary and Poland
lines.say: We're following ten countries: the four biggest economies of western Europe, three from the south, and three from central Europe: Czechia, Hungary and Poland.

lines.note: 1990 · Poland $12,821 · the lowest of the ten
lines.say: 1990. Communism in Poland has just ended. Poland's figure is 12,821 dollars a person, the lowest on this chart.
Hungary is at 21,297. Greece and Portugal, at about 27,000. And Germany, at 42,355: more than three times Poland.

card: From 1 January 1990: prices freed, support for state firms cut, the currency made convertible
lines.say: On the first of January 1990, Poland started a fast and painful reform programme, often called shock therapy. Prices were freed almost overnight, support for state firms was cut, and the currency became convertible.

lines.note: 1991: down 7% · back above the 1990 level in 1994
lines.say: The first years hurt. In 1991, the figure fell by seven percent, and unemployment rose fast. Poland only got back above its 1990 level in 1994.
But then the economy grew, and it kept on growing.
By 2000, Poland is at 18,566 dollars. Still the lowest of the ten, but its gap to Hungary has more than halved.

lines.note: 1 May 2004 · Poland joins the EU at $20,879
lines.say: 2004. Poland joins the European Union, together with nine other countries, including Czechia and Hungary. Poland's figure: 20,879 dollars a person.

card: A single market to sell into · western investment · EU funds for roads, railways and water
lines.say: Membership brought three big things. Polish firms could sell freely across the single market. Western companies built factories and offices. And EU funds paid for new roads, railways and water systems.
It also opened western job markets. Hundreds of thousands of Poles moved to work in the UK, in Ireland and later in Germany, and many of them sent money home.

lines.note: 2004 to 2008 · Poland up 22%, the fastest of the ten
lines.say: From 2004 to 2008, Poland's figure rose by 22 percent, the fastest of the ten. Czechia was close behind.
Then the financial crisis hits Europe. Watch Greece: 41,709 dollars a person in 2008, down to 37,567 by 2010. Spain falls too, and so does almost everyone else.

lines.note: 2009 · Poland grew 2.6% · every other EU economy shrank
lines.say: Poland doesn't fall. In 2009, its economy grew by two point six percent. Every other country in today's European Union shrank.

card: A large home market, a currency that fell and made exports cheaper, and EU funds that kept coming
lines.say: Economists usually point to a few reasons: a large home market that depends less on exports, a currency that fell and made Polish goods cheaper abroad, and EU money that kept on arriving.
And now, the crossings. In 2011, Poland passes Hungary.
Greece's debt crisis keeps pulling its line down. By 2013, it has lost about a quarter of its 2008 level.
In 2015, Poland passes Greece.
Then Portugal. Through the late 2010s, the gap between them halves.
In 2020, the pandemic year, Portugal's figure falls by eight percent. Poland's dips by less than one percent, and Poland moves ahead.
After the pandemic, Poland bounces straight back: up eight and a half percent in 2021 alone.
2025. Poland: 46,925 dollars a person. That's three point seven times its 1990 level, after inflation.
Spain: 49,318. Czechia, almost exactly the same. Italy and the UK, about 54,000. And Germany, 62,824.

card: Poland's GDP per person as a share of Germany's, 1990 and 2025. Of Spain's: from 40% to 95%
lines.say: Poland has gone from 30 percent of Germany's level to 75 percent, and from 40 percent of Spain's to 95.
But this line doesn't show everything. Here are three things it misses.
First, hours. In 2023, the average Polish worker worked about 1,807 hours. The average German worked 1,335. That's 472 hours more: about twelve extra forty-hour weeks.
stat: a year more than in Germany, about twelve 40-hour weeks

lines.say: Of these ten countries, only Greece works longer.
stat: Greece: the only one of the ten that works longer

lines.say: So per hour, the gap is much wider. A German worker produces about 82 dollars of output an hour. A Polish worker, about 47. Per person, Poland was at about 70 percent of Germany in 2023. Per hour worked, it was at 57.

Second, not all of Poland is catching up at the same speed. Eurostat compares regions with the EU average, per person and adjusted for prices. In 2023, the region around Warsaw was at 155 percent of that average.
Lubelskie, in the east, was at 53 percent. In 2004, the two were at 108 and 37. Both have risen, but the gap between them has grown.
Third, people. Poland's population has stayed at about 38 million since 1990. The UN's central projection has it falling to about 33 million by 2050, and to 19 million by 2100.
Fewer workers make growth harder. More of it will have to come from producing more in each hour, not from working longer.
So, what's next? Over the last ten years, Poland's figure grew by about four percent a year. Spain's grew by less than one and a half.

lines.note: Projection: Poland passes Spain in about 2 years
lines.say: If both kept that pace, and that's a big if, Poland would pass Spain in about two years. That's a simple projection, not a forecast.

lines.note: Since 1990 · Poland +3.8% a year · next: Hungary +1.9%
lines.say: In thirty-five years, Poland went from the bottom of this chart to within reach of Spain and Czechia. None of the other nine came close to its pace.

take: GDP per person, after inflation and price differences
lines.say: Three things to take away. One: Poland's GDP per person, after inflation and prices, is three point seven times what it was in 1990.

take: In 2011, 2015 and 2020. Now at 95% of Spain
lines.say: Two: it passed Hungary in 2011, Greece in 2015 and Portugal in 2020, and it's now at 95 percent of Spain.

take: Long hours, a growing gap between regions, and a shrinking population
lines.say: Three: the catch-up isn't finished. Poles work long hours, Warsaw has pulled far ahead of the east, and the population is set to shrink.
